text:
Dear Dr. Henderson,

Thank you for agreeing to see this 33-year-old woman for a comprehensive review. Her medical background is notable for intermittent hematologic follow-up dating back to early childhood, with initial concerns documented around two years of age.

Her recent laboratory evaluation revealed a pronounced macrocytic anemia, with the peripheral smear demonstrating prominent megaloblastic changes and multi-segmented neutrophils. Corresponding nutritional markers showed a strikingly depressed serum cobalamin level. In addition, routine urinary screening showed significant protein loss, which was subsequently verified on repeat testing as an ongoing urinary protein excretion. 

Her physical assessment is otherwise entirely normal. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, heart rate is 70 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Cardiopulmonary auscultation is clear, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender without hepatosplenomegaly or lower-extremity swelling. A focused neurological examination, including sensory testing, vibration sense, and deep tendon reflexes, revealed no abnormalities. She works full-time in administrative logistics, does not smoke, and drinks alcohol only on social occasions. Her family history is non-contributory, and her only routine medication is a standard oral contraceptive.

Given the combination of low circulating cobalamin, megaloblastic red cell lineage, and persistent urinary protein excretion stemming from early childhood, I would be grateful for your expert opinion and recommendations on how best to proceed with her evaluation. 

Sincerely,

Dr. Evelyn Vance
Internal Medicine Associates
